to the stoichiometry, while the excess oxygen is attributed to RGO and adsorbed water
molecules as verified by XPS studies.
TEM and HRTEM analyses were employed to explore the detailed microstructure of the
2D/2D/2D BWO/RGO/CN heterojunction with reference to BWO, RGO, and CN. As shown

columns: in Fig. S5a, CN clearly exhibits a flat 2D layered structure composed of a few thin nanosheets,

Notably, the TEM image of BRC-15 (Fig. 4a) clearly displayed even disposition of the BWO

these results, it can be inferred that the highly-segregated BWO nanosheets in the reaction R
solution are strongly attached to the RGO/CN during the hydrothermal process, which leads to

the formation of BWO/RGO/CN heterojunctions with highly effective 2D/2D/2D S

[28]. The other lattice fringes spaced by 0.32 nm belong to the typical (002) planes of CN [27].

T

5. Conclusions
In summary, various binary semiconductor/ZIF photocatalysts
(TiO2/ZIF-8) have been fabricated with the help of the grinding
method and the solid synthesis method. The photocatalysts
prepared by the grinding method exhibit better photocatalytic
performances than those of the photocatalysts fabricated by the
solid synthesis method. The experimental nding demonstrates
that diﬀerent synthetic methods result in varied photocatalytic
performances, caused by their diﬀerent structural features. The
resulting exhibits enhanced photocatalytic TiO2/ZIF-8-GX

Therefore, a great deal of research has been dedicated to improving the performance

of titania, such as surface modiﬁcation [18], doping [19], coupling with other materials [20],
as well as optimization of physicochemical properties via varying preparation [21] and
treatment conditions [22]. Various factors that affect the photocatalytic activity have
been reported, including crystal structure (anatase or rutile), particle size, surface area,
and the presence of surface hydroxyls [23-25]. These properties can be easily altered via
heat treatment of the TiO2 in various gas atmospheres. For instance, high-temperature
treatment in air was reported to intensify phase transformation from anatase to rutile and
to decrease speciﬁc surface area and concentration of surface hydroxyls [26-28].
In most of the studies, the attempt is made to correlate the photocatalytic activity with
only one or a few physical properties of the photocatalyst. Generally, it can be concluded
that the most prominent effect on the photocatalytic activity provides the coexistence of
several titania polymorphs. This effect is usually assigned to a lower energy gap of the
it is also worth mentioning mixed phase TiO2 than that of pure phases [29]. However,
that despite the lower band gap of pure rutile, anatase exhibits better photocatalytic
properties [30]. This effect indicates that other properties, apart from the band gap, also
effect the photocatalytic performance. Particularly, it was hypothesized that the good
is due to the transfer of photo-generated photocatalytic activity of mixed-phase TiO2
electrons from anatase to a lower energy rutile electron-trapping site. This electron transfer
reduces the recombination rate of anatase by increasing the separation between the electron
and hole, resulting in greater photocatalytic reactivity [31-33]. More interestingly, T. Bak
et al. investigated the effect of several defect-related properties, including the concentration
of surface-active sites, the Fermi level, the charge transport, and the band gap of pure TiO2
on its photocatalytic performance in the oxidation of methylene blue [34]. The obtained
results indicated that the photocatalytic activity of TiO2 was inﬂuenced signiﬁcantly by
the concentration of surface-active sites and Fermi level while the band gap and charge
transport had a minor impact [34]. The effect of speciﬁc surface on the photocatalytic
It can be hypothesized properties of TiO2 is also not as straightforward as it may seem.
that the high speciﬁc area is beneﬁcial as it improves the adsorption of the target molecules
onto the surface of titania [25,35].
However, recently, we have shown that during the photocatalytic reduction of carbon
dioxide, the TiO2 deactivates reversibly due to the slow desorption and consequent accumu-
lation of reaction products on its surface [36]. This indicates that the high speciﬁc surface
area of TiO2 may, on the contrary, be a negative factor affecting its photocatalytic activity.
Therefore, great care is needed in drawing conclusions on the decisive factors of activity
in photocatalytic reactions and in rationalizing the correlations between photocatalytic
properties of a semiconductor and its physicochemical properties.
The work is aimed to evaluate separately the inﬂuence of each physicochemical prop-
erty of TiO2 on its photocatalytic performance in the gas-phase CO2 reduction. The prop-
erties of titania, such as phase composition, speciﬁc surface area, and band gap energy,
were tuned by adjusting calcination temperature. Special attention was given to the ini-
tial adsorption of carbon dioxide on the surface of titania and subsequent desorption of
photocatalytic products.
2. Results and Discussion
2.1. Physicochemical Properties of Pristine and Calcinated TiO2 Samples
The results of physicochemical characterization of TiO2 samples are summarized
in Table 1. According to the obtained results, the raw TiO2 had a speciﬁc surface area
(SSA BET) of about 57 m2. It contained mainly anatase phase (88%) with crystallite
size of 18 nm and possessed a band gap of 3.291 eV, which is close to that reported
elsewhere [37,38].

2.2. Photocatalytic and Adsorption Properties of TiO2 Samples
The results of the photocatalytic measurements showed that the investigated samples
at ambient temperature easily underwent deactivation, as can be seen by the sharp
decrease of methanol formation rate with time on stream (Figure 4). The only exception
was the TiO2-C1000 sample which demonstrated relatively stable photocatalytic activity
over the 5 h. As was discussed previously, the deactivation of the photocatalysts in this
process can be due to the accumulation of reaction products on the surface of the
photocatalyst hindering the adsorption of reagents [36]. The IR measurements indeed
showed that the formed methoxy groups (2819, 2897, and 2922 cm-1) hardly desorbed from
the surface of photocatalysts irrespective of their specific surface area (Figure 5B). For
example, according to the FTIR measurements, approximately only 35% of total adsorbed
methanol desorbs from the surface of pristine TiO2 when purged with inert gas for 1 h
under UV-VIS irradiation (Figure 6). In the case of TiO2-C700, about 45% of organic
groups were removed under the same conditions, while in the case of TiO2-C1000 it was
above 65%. Nevertheless, it is worth mentioning that the observed deactivation of
photocatalysts is reversible as they can be partially regenerated by heating at 300 °C in the

The XPS spectra were measured using a VG ESCALAB HP photoelectron spectrometer
(Thermo Electron North America LLC, Waltham, MA, USA) with a non-monochromated
primary radiation source (MgKα line of hν = 1253.6 eV) with a power 150 W. Sample pow-
ders were pressed into pills (7 × 15 mm, 2 mm). Before the experiments, the spectrometer
binding energy (BE) scale was calibrated based on the energy position of metallic gold
Au4f7/2 (84.0 eV) and copper Cu2p3/2 (932.7 eV) lines. A titanium Ti2p3/2 line with a
maximum at a binding energy 458.6 eV was used as an internal standard [47]. To analyze
the quantitative composition of the samples and the chemical state of the elements on the
surface, the core-level spectra of the elements (Ti2p, C1, O1s) were recorded. The mea-
surement accuracy of XPS binding energy was 0.1 eV. The spectra were ﬁtted with the
individual components using the Gauss and Lorentz functions after Shirley background
subtraction. The spectra were processed using XPS-Calc software (Thermo Electron North
America LLC, Waltham, MA, USA) tested previously on model catalytic systems [48] and
dispersed powder catalysts [49].
The diffuse reﬂectance spectra of the powder samples were measured using Cary
5000 UV-VIS-NIR spectrophotometer with an integrating sphere (Agilent, Santa Clara,
CA, USA) in the 200-800 nm wavelength range. Reﬂectance spectra were recorded with a
spectral resolution of 1 nm.
The adsorption-desorption measurements were performed using IR Tracer-100 FTIR
spectrometer (Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan) equipped with an MCT detector. During the
experiments, the 5% CO2-95% Ar and 5% CH3OH-95% Ar mixtures were used. The gas
ﬂow rate was 10 mL/min. The desorption rate of adsorbed methanol was calculated as
a change or area of corresponding IR peaks during the purging with an inert gas under
UV-VIS irradiation. All measurements were performed at 30 ◦C.
The surface morphology of the investigated samples was studied by HITACHI scan-
ning electron microscope (Hitachi High-Tech, Tokyo, Japan), equipped with EDS energy
dispersive spectrometer (Thermo Noran, Worona Road Madison, WI, USA).
3.3. Photocatalytic Activity Measurement
A detailed description of a photocatalytic reactor has been given elsewhere [36].
Brieﬂy, the photocatalytic reduction of CO2 was performed in a ﬂow reactor equipped
with a cooling jacket, a heater, and a quartz window. Two paired, high-pressure mercury
lamps (POLAMP LRF 400W) were used as a source of UV-VIS light. The area of TiO2
surface exposed to UV-vis irradiation was 10.18 cm2. For performing the photocatalytic
tests under either UV or visible light irradiation alone, special cutoff ﬁlters were applied.
The surface area exposed to the irradiation, in this case, was equal to 2.01 cm2. The process
conditions were as follows: the temperature of the semiconductors-30 and 100 ◦C; the re-
action mixture-5% vol. H2O/95% vol. CO2; and total gas ﬂow-0.8 mL/min. The ﬁrst
measurements were taken after at least 2 h on stream. The analysis of reaction products
was carried out by an on-line gas chromatograph equipped with a ﬂame ionization detector
and a capillary HP PLOT/Q column. The yield of an organic compound was calculated
according to the following equation:

4. Conclusions
The physical properties of titanium oxide, such as the surface morphology and com-
position and the adsorption of electromagnetic radiation and reaction reagents, can be
controlled to some extent by varying the temperature of the calcination process. The in-
crease in calcination temperature resulted in an increase in particle size (decrease of speciﬁc
surface area), a higher concentration of surface hydroxyls, and a lower band-gap energy
(at 700 ◦C due to anatase-rutile phase transformation). The activity of TiO2 samples in the
process of photocatalytic reduction of CO2 at room temperature was found to be dependent
primarily on the rate of desorption of reaction products from the surface of TiO2. The sam-
ples with a high speciﬁc surface area (above 16 m2/g) easily underwent deactivation with
time on stream due to the accumulation of reaction products, while the sample with a
low speciﬁc area (4 m2/g) demonstrated relatively stable photocatalytic activity over the
5 h. On the other hand, when the process was performed at 100 ◦C (the adsorption factor
is partially suppressed) the low speciﬁc surface was found to be negatively impacting
the photocatalytic activity of the investigated samples. The most important factor, un-
der such conditions, was improved utilization of visible light irradiation. This was the
main reason for the enhanced photocatalytic activity of rutile in comparison to that of
anatase/rutile mixture. To summarize, one of the most essential factors that should be
considered while developing highly active photocatalysts for gas-phase reduction of carbon
dioxide is ﬁnding the optimal trade-off between its adsorption and desorption properties.

columns: Keywords: CO2 photocatalytic reduction; Codoping; TiO2; Photoreactor; Simulated sunlight
rows: Introduction
Global warming and energy shortage are two major problems which the world is facing nowadays.
One of the best solutions to the above issues is to convert greenhouse gas (mainly CO2) into solar fuels,
which can mitigate global warming and provide valuable fuels simultaneously [1-3]. Since Inoue et al. [4]
first reported CO2 photocatalytic reduction on semiconductors in 1979, a variety of semiconductors such
as TiO2 [5-7], ZnO [8, 9], CeO2 [10, 11], C3N4 [12], and WO3 [13, 14] have been applied for CO2
photocatalytic reduction. Among them, TiO2 is one of the most promising photocatalysts due to its high
activity, good photostability, low cost, and environmental friendliness [15-17]. However, TiO2 still suffers
from low reaction efficiency, low utilization of visible light, fast recombination of photogenerated

columns: It has been reported that doping foreign atoms into TiO2 can effectively improve the photocatalytic
rows: activity of TiO2 because the dopants can promote the separation of photogenerated charges and extend the
light absorption region towards visible light [21, 22]. For example, Wu et al. [23] reported that V doping
narrowed the band gap of TiO2 and effectively enhanced the activity of V doped TiO2 catalyst. Tahir [24]
found that In doping could effectively inhibited the recombination of photogenerated charges and
enhanced the photocatalytic activity of TiO2 for CO2 reduction. Recently, codoping has been recognized
to be a more useful approach to improve the photocatalytic activity of TiO2 than single element doping
due to the synergy of different dopants [22, 25]. Many different elements including V-N [26], V-Ag [27],
W-C [25] and Mo-C [28] were combined and codoped into TiO2 to improve its photocatalytic activity. In
our previous work [29], we found that W doped TiO2 exhibited high photocatalytic activity under UV
light irradiation while V doping greatly enhanced the visible light activity of TiO2. Thus, it is possible to
achieve a highly efficient visible-light driven photocatalyst by codoping V and W into TiO2. However,
few studies have considered the effect of V and W codoping on the photocatalytic CO2 reduction of TiO2.

columns: reduction activity of TiO2 was investigated in a internal-illuminated honeycomb photoreactor. The roles
rows: of V and W were discussed in the CO2 photocatalytic reduction. Finally, a possible mechanism of CO2
photocatalytic reduction was proposed over V and W doped TiO2 catalyst.
2. Experimental
2.1. Catalyst preparation and coating process
X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the catalysts were recorded on an Empyrean diffractometer using
Cu Kα radiation (λ = 0.1542 nm) in the range of 10-80 °. The surface morphology and elemental mapping
of the catalysts were examined by environment scanning electron microscopy (ESEM) with an FEI Quanta
200 instrument. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images of the catalysts were obtained by using
an FEI Tecnai G2 F30 instrument. The specific surface areas and pore size distribution of the catalysts
were measured by a Micrometrics ASAP 2020 surface area and porosity analyzer. X-ray photoelectron
spectra (XPS) of the catalysts were recorded on a Shimadzu/KRATOS AXIS-ULTRA DLD-600W
instrument equipped with Al/Mg Kα radiation. Photoluminescence (PL) and Raman spectra of the
catalysts were recorded on a confocal laser Raman microscope (Horiba JobinYvon, LabRAM HR800) by
using a 325 nm and a 532 nm excitation light source, respectively. The UV-Vis absorbance spectra of the

columns: by a gas chromatography (GC) equipped with an on-line sampling loop (1 mL), a flame ionization detector (FID), (and a thermal conductivity detector (TCD). First, the effluents were pre-separated by a carbon molecular sieve)
rows: (TDX-01) column to flush CO2 to atmosphere. Then the effluents flowed through a molecular sieve 5A column
for the separation of H2, O2, N2, CH4, and CO. Finally, H2 in the effluents was analyzed by the TCD detector and
CH4 and CO (converted to CH4 by a methanizer) were analyzed by the FID detector. Ar was used as the carrier
gas.

rows: and V3W3T were all smaller than that of pristine TiO2, which demonstrated that V and W doping inhibited
the growth of TiO2 grains. Similar results were reported in the literatures [26]. No V or W species were
detected by XRD, which can be attributed to the low concentration of V and W doping. It is notable that
the anatase (101) peak of V3T, W3T, and V3W3T shifts towards the higher diffraction angle, indicating
that V and W ions might incorporate into the lattice of anatase TiO2 and substituted for Ti4+.

rows: XPS was used to investigate the chemical states of Ti, O, V and W on the surface of the catalysts. Fig. 4A
shows the high-resolution Ti 2p XPS spectra of the samples. There exist two peaks in the binding energy region
of Ti 2p. The binding energies of Ti 2p3/2 for pristine TiO2 and W3T are around 458.6 eV, which indicates Ti4+ in
pristine TiO2 and W3T [38, 39]. Notably, comparing with pristine TiO2, the binding energy of Ti 2p3/2 for V3T
shifted to a negative value, suggesting that some of Ti4+ is reduced to Ti3+. This phenomenon can be attributed to
the substitution of Ti4+ by the doped V4+ and the formation of Ti-O-V bonds [26, 40], which could induce defects
in the TiO2 lattice, leading to the reduction of Ti4+ into Ti3+ or the formation of oxygen vacancies [27]. The
formation of Ti3+ in V doped TiO2 were also observed by Pham et al. [27] and Wang et al. [36] and they owed it
to the the incorporation of vanadium ions into the TiO2 lattice. However, for V3W3T, the Ti 2p binding energy
shifted back to around 458.6 eV. This indicated that W doping inhibited the reduction of Ti4+. The high-resolution
O 1s XPS spectra of all the samples in Fig. 4B can be resolved into two peaks. The one with lower energy is
assigned to oxygen in TiO2 lattice (OL) and the other one can be ascribed to superficial oxygen of hydroxyl
species (OH) [17]. The binding energy of O 1s peak for V3T is also lower than that of pristine TiO2, indicating the
electron transfers from V to TiO2.
Fig. 4C shows the high-resolution V 2p XPS spectra of V3T and V3W3T catalysts, which can be resolved
into two peaks. The peak at around 517.0 eV could be ascribed to V5+ [26], whereas that at around 515.8 eV was
assigned to V4+ [27]. Combining the results of XRD and Raman spectra, V4+ ions could substitute for Ti4+ ions to
form a Ti-O-V bond in the TiO2 lattice while the V5+ could exist in the form of V2O5 on the surface of TiO2,
resulting from much closer radii between Ti4+ (74.5 pm) and V4+ (72.0 pm) than V5+ (68.0 pm) [36]. Similar
results have also been reported by other researchers [27, 41, 42]. The concentration of V5+ was much higher than
that of V4+ for both V3T and V3W3T catalysts, demonstrating that V5+ was dominant on the surface of V3T and
V3W3T catalyst. In addition, W doping does not show obvious influence on the chemical state of V. The W 4f
region displays two peaks at 37.4 and 35.4 eV (Fig. 4D), which can be ascribed to the W 4f5/2 and W4f7/2 for W6+

The UV-Vis absorbance spectra of the catalysts are shown in Fig. 7A. The absorption edges of V3T
and V3W3T catalysts exhibited red shift compared to that of pristine TiO2 and W3T, indicating V doping
could enhance the visible light absorption of TiO2. The band gap of the samples was calculated by using
(Ahν)n = k(hν-Eg), where A is the absorbance, k is the parameter that related to the effective masses
associated with the valence and conduction bands, n is 2 for an indirect transition, hν is the absorption
energy, and Eg is the band gap [5]. Fig. 7B shows the function of (Ahν)2 to hν, and Eg of the samples was
summarized in Table 1. The band gap of pristine TiO2 was lower than that of anatase TiO2 (3.2 eV) due
to the smaller band gap of rutile TiO2 than anatase TiO2 [45]. The band gap of V3T is smaller than that of

columns: visible light absorption of V doped TiO2. Nevertheless, the band gaps of W3T and V3W3T were very
rows: close to pristine TiO2 and V3T catalyst, respectively. Although W doping could enhance the visible light
absorption of anatase TiO2 [43, 44], it inhibited the formation of rutile TiO2. As a result, the band gap of
pristine TiO2 and V3T changed very little after W doping.

rows: determined to be TiO2 according to EDS analysis. This indicated successful loading of TiO2 catalysts on
the honeycomb support.
Fig. 11 illustrates the SEM images and corresponding EDS analysis of the cross-section of TiO2
coating layer on the honeycomb support. Obviously, many pores can be observed on the cross-section of
honeycomb support, while the first 30 um thick has a higher density, which can be attributed to the coating
layer. The EDS line mapping exhibits most Ti element was distributed from 0 to 30 um deep, indicating
the coating thickness was ca. 30 nm. This further indicated successful coating of TiO2 catalyst on the
honeycomb support.
3.3. CO2 photocatalytic reduction
CO2 photocatalytic reduction over V3W3T catalyst under simulated sunlight irradiation was performed in the
honeycomb reactor and conventional reactor, respectively. Fig. 12 shows the CO, CH4, and H2 yields in the above
two cases. As shown in Fig. 12, the yields of products from honeycomb reactor were much higher than those from
conventional reactor. This can be attributed to the high surface area per unit volume provided by the honeycomb
support and efficient utilization of light irradiation via optical fibers [30, 31].
Fig. 13 and Table 2 shows the effect of V and W doping on the photocatalytic CO2 reduction activity and
quantum efficiency of TiO2 catalyst in the honeycomb reactor. H2, CO, and CH4 were found to be the main
products and CO was dominant among all the products. The activity of pristine TiO2 was lowest among all the
samples and both V and W doping enhanced the production of H2, CO, and CH4. The highest photocatalytic
activity was obtained by V3W3T, whose CO, CH4, and H2 yields were 1.91, 0.22, and 0.27 umol g-1 h-1,
respectively. There is no doubt that the large surface area of V3W3T is helpful for the high photocatalytic activity.
However, the quantum efficiency of V3W3T is only 4.5 times as many as that of pristine TiO2 while the BET
surface area of the former is almost 13 times as many as that of the latter. Moreover, the photocatalytic activity of
W3T is smaller than that of V3T although its larger surface area than V3T. Therefore, the large surface area is not
the main reason for the highest activity of V3W3T and the main reason can be the promoted charge separation

columns: caused by V and W doping and enhanced visible light absorption by V doping, as evident in PL and UV-Vis
rows: analysis. The V4+ and W6+ ions doped in TiO2 lattice can capture photogenerated electrons and accelerate the
electron transfer within TiO2 [26, 27, 44]. Meanwhile, the V5+ on the surface of TiO2 can trap photogenerated
electrons and transferred them to CO2 adsorbed on the surface of TiO2 [26, 40]. As a result, photogenerated
charges were separated effectively. In addition, V4+ doping caused the formation of an intermediate state within
the band gap of TiO2 [26, 27], which enables TiO2 to be excited by visible light irradiation.

columns: heterojunction and the W6+ doped in TiO2 lattice can work as electron traps, the excited electrons on the CB of
rows: TiO2 can be captured by V2O5 and W6+ [26, 44] while the photogenerated holes are left in the VB of TiO2,
resulting in effective separation of photogenerated electron-hole pairs, as evident in PL analysis. Then these
trapped electrons react with CO2 and water adsorbed on the surface of the catalyst to produce solar fuels, resulting
in enhanced CO2 photocatalytic reduction.

rows: pristine TiO2 and single metal doped TiO2 catalysts. The V and W codoped TiO2 catalyst exhibited enhanced
photocatalytic activity comparing with pristine TiO2 and single metal doped TiO2 catalysts, which could be
attributed to the enhanced visible light absorption and promoted separation of photogenerated electron-hole pairs
caused by V and W codoping. The V and W codoped TiO2 also exhibited good cycle performance due to the
stable chemical states of V and W during photocatalytic reaction.

Abstract
Controlled fabrication of Ti3C2 MXene with unique topology and layered bentonite (Bt) nanoclay
to construct a 2D/2D/2D g-C3N4/Bt/Ti3C2 MXene heterojunction for intriguing photocatalytic CO2
reduction has been investigated. The MXene/Bt composite exhibits high-light absorption and
faster charges separation and transportation. The photoactivity of 2D/2D Ti3C2/g-C3N4 of 1.38
folds higher
than bulk Ti3AlC2/g-C3N4 obtained due
to
intimate
interface
interaction with
proficient charges separation. The highest g-C3N4/Bt/Ti3C2 heterojunction activity for CH4
evolution of 4.18, 4.42 and 6.96 folds more was achieved compared with g-C3N4/Ti3C3, Bt/g-C3N4
and g-C3N4, respectively. This boosted activity was evidently due to Ti3C2/g-C3N4 Schottky
junction with Bt-mediator to provide new electron transfer channels. More interestingly, with
proton rich acetic-acid reagent, 4.15 folds more CH4 production than using only water under
prolonged stability was observed. Thus, this study provides a promising approach for clean energy
system and potential applications of MXenes/Bt materials for solar fuels production.
Keywords: Photocatalytic CO2 reduction; Bentonite green clay; g-C3N4, Ti3C2 MXene; Schottky
junction; CO2 methanation
1. Introduction
Global warming due to increasing CO2 level in the atmosphere and excessive use of fossil fuels
result in depleting the energy reserves and is a major cause of global warming. Among the potential
approaches, conversion of CO2 to useful chemicals and fuels is promising to mitigate greenhouse
effects in addition of producing renewable energy [1, 2]. Recently, photocatalysis, in the presence
of light energy and low cost feedstock (CO2 and water) enables single step conversion of CO2 to
value added products such as CO, CH4, CH3OH, HCHO and HCOOH in the presence of
semiconductor materials, thus deems the most promising route towards solving energy and

columns: environmental problems [3, 4]. Among the semiconductors, TiO2 has been widely explored due to (its several benefits such as low-cost, high stability and suitable oxidation potential. However, it)
rows: presents lower catalytic activity due to charge carrier recombination in addition of wide band gap
energy and active only under UV-light irradiation [5, 6]. Therefore, it would be promising to
explore structured semiconductors materials to maximize solar driven CO2 reduction to renewable
fuels.
Polymeric structured graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4) is a promising semiconductor due to its
several advantages such as visible light active, cheap and easy to prepare, higher chemical/thermal
stability and suitable reduction potential for the production of several chemicals [7, 8]. However,
g-C3N4 has limitations such as lower photoactivity due to faster charge carrier recombination rate
in addition of smaller surface area [9]. Several approaches such as surface modification, O-doping,
metals loading and coupling with other semiconductors have been investigated to maximize g-
C3N4 activity towards selective CO2 reduction [10, 11]. For example, Mg/g-C3N4 for CO2
reduction to CO and CH4 [12], Mn-Cu/g-C3N4 for CO2 conversion to CH4 [13], and Ag-La/g-C3N4
for CO2 reduction to CO/H2 has been investigated [14]. Obviously, several metal/semiconductor
composite systems have been tested to improve activity of g-C3N4, however, this system is not
much proficient in addition of uneconomical due to high cost of using metals. Alternatively, g-
C3N4 activity can also be boosted using low cost and environmentally friendly green clays due to
their layered structure and have larger active surface area and superior sorption process.
Clay minerals are the class of crystalline materials, which consist of pillared interlayered structure.
Among the layered clay materials, montmorillonite (Mt) and bentonite (Bt) are the most popular
due to their several advantages such as high surface area, availability in abundance, low-cost,
porous structure, and high stability under the mild reaction conditions [15, 16]. Coupling these
clays with other semiconductors provide higher dispersion and faster charges separation. Using
2D layered-clay with 2D g-C3N4 would have a good 2D/2D interfacial interaction, enabling higher
CO2 adsorption and faster charge carrier separation [17]. This is obviously due to cat-ions (M+) in
the layered structure and provides charge trapping ability [18, 19]. Several research articles report
the use of Mt to promote semiconductor TiO2 photo-activity in water splitting and CO2 reduction
applications. We investigated the use of Ni/TiO2 dispersed with Mt for CO2 reduction with
enhanced activity and products selectivity [20]. Compared to Mt, Bt has good crystalline and
mesoporous structure with higher CO2 uptake during the adsorption process [21]. However, there

columns: are limited reports available on the use of Bt in the photocatalytic CO2 reduction applications.
rows: Recently, pillared bentonite with enhanced electrocatalytic CO2 reduction has been reported [22].
Similarly, Ni/bentonite has been explored for thermal catalytic CO2 methanation with 100 %
selectivity of CH4 production [23]. Therefore, it would be promising to investigate 2D/2D Bt/g-
C3N4 composite for photocatalytic CO2 methanation under visible light irradiation. According to
available literature, the use of layered 2D Bt dispersed with g-C3N4 has never been investigated
for photocatalytic CO2 conversion applications.
Recently, Mxenes, a novel family of two dimensional (2D) nanomaterials have stimulated growing
concern in improving photocatalytic activity of semiconductor materials [24-26]. Among them,
Ti3C2 is a typical Mxene and has been widely investigated because of its unique features such as
low cost, good electrical conductivity, high structural stability, and promising visible light
capturing [27, 28]. More importantly, 2D Ti3C2 Mxene can be combined with semiconductor
materials to develop Schottky junctions, which effectively promotes charge carrier separation.
Thus, in addition of Ti3C2 application in the field of batteries and supercapacitors, they have great
potential for photocatalysis [29]. In this perspective, Low et al. [30] demonstrated that Ti3C2 could
remarkably promote activity of TiO2/Mxene Ti3C2 composite for excellent photocatalytic CO2
reduction to CH4. This can be ascribed to excellent electrical conductivity and faster charge carrier
separation. Besides, Zhuang et al. [31] also found that TiO2/Ti3C2 composite exhibited enhanced
activity towards hydrogen production due to proficient charge carrier separation. Benefiting from
the good electrical conductivity of Ti3C2, significantly enhanced hydrogen production over the
ZnO/Ti3C2 composite was obtained [32]. Theoretically, a Schottky junction could be established
by coupling metal with higher work function than the work function of n-type semiconductor. As
the Ti3C2 work function is greater than the work function of g-C3N4, they can be combined to
develop 2D/2D Ti3C2/g-C3N4 heterojunction composite, thus would enable efficient visible light
absorption and superior charge carrier separation [33, 34]. By introducing 2D Bt with Ti3C2/g-
C3N4 to construct a 2D/2D/2D heterojunction will be a promising system for maximizing charges
separation with enhanced catalytic activity under visible light.
In this work, novel design and fabrication of Bt mediated Ti3C2/g-C3N4 Schottky junction for
selective photocatalytic CO2 reduction to fuels under visible light has been explored. Successful
development of 2D/2D/2D g-C3N4/Bt/T3C2 heterojunction with superior interfacial transfer of
photgenerated charges in the hybrid composite was achieved. The performance of bulk 2D MAX

columns: Ti3AlC2 and monolayer 2D Ti3C2 were further explored to understand their charges separation
rows: efficiency. Similarly, the role of UV and visible light irradiation on the photoactivity of g-
C3N4/Bt/T3C2 heterojunction for dynamic photocatalytic CO2 reduction to CO and CH4 was further
investigated. Based on the experimental results, introduction of Bt into g-C3N4/Ti3C2 composite
found very promising for maximizing CO2 methanation. To further understand the mechanism and
route of methane formation, g-C3N4/Bt/T3C2 photoactivity was stimulated with reaction system
enriched with protons through introducing acetic acid. The thermodynamic aspects were further
discussed to understand the role of hydrogen in the reaction system with water splitting competing
reaction during CO2 reduction process. Finally, stability analysis was conducted in consecutive
cycles to inspect catalyst life for continuous CO2 reduction to fuels.
2. Experimental
2.1 Materials
Melamine (Merck, 99.99 %) for synthesis of g-C3N4, Bentonite (Sigma Aldrich, 99.99 %), titanium
aluminum carbide (Ti3AlC2, >98%, 200 mesh, Famouschem China) for the synthesis of Ti3C2,
methanol (Merck, 99.99%) and hydrofluoric acid (HF, 49 %, Emplura) are the materials and
chemicals used in this study.
2.2 Synthesis of Ti3C2 MXenes
The Ti3C2 MXenes nanosheets were synthesized through etching of Ti3AlC2 with HF in a
continuous stirred tank reactor. Typically, 1 g of Ti3AlC2 (powder) was dispersed in a 20 mL HF
solution (content ≥ 49 %) and suspension was transferred into Teflon lined stainless steel reactor
and stirred for 24 h to get Ti3C2 MXenes. The suspension obtained was centrifuged and washed
with DI water until pH ≥ 6. The product obtained was dried at 100 oC for 24 in an oven under
airflow and named as Ti3C2 MXenes nanosheets. The Ti3C2 MXenes with in-situ growth of TiO2
NPs was achieved by increasing etching time to 96 h and named as Ti3C2Tx Mxenes nanosheets.
2.3 Synthesis of g-C3N4 nanosheets
The g-C3N4 was prepared using melamine as the precursor through hydrothermal approach
according to our previous report [10]. First, melamine (10 g) was placed in a ceramic crucible,
covered with lid and heated in a furnace at 550 oC for 2 h under air atmosphere. After cooling,
yellowish color bulk cake obtained was grinded to fine powder using mortar and pestle. Then, the
powder was added into 40 mL (1M) nitric acid solution and stirred for next 24 h. The suspension

columns: obtained was centrifuged and washed with water to remove impurities and to get pH ≥7. Finally,
rows: sample obtained was dried at 100 oC overnight and named as graphitic carbon nitride nanosheets
2.4 Synthesis of g-C3N4/Bt/Ti3C2 MXene composite
The g-C3N4/Bt, g-C3N4/Ti3C2 MXene and g-C3N4/Bt/Ti3C2 MXene composite samples were
prepared through ultrasonic approach at normal temperature. First, g-C3N4 (1 g) was dispersed into
20 mL methanol and stirred for 6 h to get uniform dispersion of g-C3N4 nanosheets (sample A).
Second, specific amount of bentonite (Bt) was added to 20 mL methanol under stirring and
ultrasonic for 60 min to get exfoliated Bt nanosheets (sample B). Third, Ti3C2 added in 20 mL
methanol was dispersed through ultrasonic to get exfoliated Ti3C2 layers (sample C). In the next
stage, Bt suspension (sample B) was added to g-C3N4 suspension (sample A) and stirred for 6 h
with ultrasonic for 60 min to get good interface interaction of g-C3N4 with Bt (sample D). The
sample obtained was centrifuged and dried at 100 oC for 24 h and named as 2D/2D g-C3N4/Bt
composite. Similarly, for the synthesis of g-C3N4/Ti3C2 MXene composite, the Ti3C2 (sample C)
suspension was added to g-C3N4 suspension (sample A) under continuous stirring. The product
obtained was oven dried at 100 oC under air flow and named as 2D/2D g-C3N4/Ti3C2 MXene
composite. Finally, g-C3N4/Bt/Ti3C2 MXene composite was synthesized using the similar method
as discussed above. Firstly, g-C3N4 solution (sample A) was mixed with Bt suspension (sample B)
to get homogenous dispersion of both the samples (sample D). Afterwards, specific amount of
Ti3C2 dispersed in methanol (sample C) was added to mixture of g-C3N4/Bt (sample D) under
stirring. The sample was further ultrasonic for 60 min to get good dispersion of nanosheets and
finally centrifuged to remove methanol. The sludge obtained was dried for 24 h at 100 oC and
named a 2D/2D/2D g-C3N4/Bt/Ti3C2 MXene composite nanosheets. The scheme for the synthesis
of 2D/2D/2D g-C3N4/Bt/Ti3C2 MXene composite has been demonstrated in Fig. 1.

2.6 Photoactivity test
The performance analysis of photocatalysts was conducted in a fixed bed photoreactor operated
under visible light irradiation. The source of light was a 35 W HID lamp with a maximum light
intensity 20 mW cm-2 with wavelength 420 nm. The experiments were conducted with and without
UV-cut filters located above the glass window and their effects on catalyst performance and
products selectivity were evaluated. A solar concentrator was used to simulate light irradiations
from the lamp towards the catalyst surface. The reactor was fixed with a glass window of thickness
10 mm and lamp integrated with a concentrator mirror was located 5 cm above the glass window.
First, 150 mg powder catalyst was uniformly distributed at the reactor bottom and then nitrogen
(N2) gas was passed through the reactor to remove air and other impurities from the reactor.
Second, high purity CO2 (99.99%), regulated by mass flow controller (MFC), was bubbled through
the water saturator to carry moisture and was flowing through the reactor for 30 min to saturate
the catalyst and to purge the reactor system. All the experiments were conducted under reactor
pressure of 0.20 bars above the atmospheric pressure. The CO2/H2O feed ratio was varied using
different temperature of water saturator (e.g., 15, 30 and 45 oC), while kept constant CO2 flow rate
(20 mL min-1) in all the experiments. Similarly, for the investigation of acetic acid effect on the

3.2.1 Effect of catalyst loading on CO2 reduction with H2O
The photocatalytic activity of different catalysts for the production of CO and CH4 during photo-
reduction of CO2 with water under visible light irradiation is presented in Fig. 7. As depicted in
Fig. 7 (a) carbon monoxide (CO) is the main CO2 reduction product accompanied by appreciable
amount of methane (CH4) production. Using pristine g-C3N4, a weak photoactivity with CO and
CH4 evolution rate of 76 and 33 umole g-cat-1 h-1, respectively were produced. This was obviously
due to faster recombination of photo-generated electrons (e-) and holes (h+) pairs. Increasing
photoactivity of g-C3N4 was obtained after coupling with Bt to construct 2D/2D g-C3N4/Bt
heterojunction. Using g-C3N4/Bt composite, CO evolution rate of 285 umole g-cat-1 h-1 was
observed, a 3.75-fold higher than using pristine g-C3N4 sheets. This obvious enhancement was due
to the formation of 2D/2D interaction, enabling superior charges separation and their transportation
within the catalyst surface. Previously, we investigated montmorillonite (Mt) clay dispersed TiO2
composites for photocatalytic CO2 reduction and water splitting applications and witnessed similar
outcomes [43, 44]. Therefore, significantly enhanced photoactivity was apparently due to good
interaction between g-C3N4 and Bt with superior charge carrier separation due to layered structure
of Bt, resulting in efficient photocatalytic CO2 reduction to CO and CH4.

3.2.2 Effect of UV and visible light irradiations
The light source has a significant contribution to alter the performance of photocatalyst, g-
C3N4/Bt/Ti3C2 composite catalyst was further evaluated under different visible light sources and
results are demonstrated in Fig. 8 (a). Obviously, productions trends of CO and CH4 are different
using visible light irradiations under UV-cut filters (ʎ≥420 nm) and without filters. Using UV-cut
filter, lower amount of CH4 was produced, which was significantly increased under visible light
irradiation without UV-filters. The CH4 evolution of 101 umol g-cat-1 was obtained under UV-cut
filters, which was increased by 4.6 folds higher (460 umol g-cat-1) without UV-cut filters.
Similarly, production of CO was increased by 1.3 folds higher without UV-cut filters. These
findings could be explained based on the availability of total light intensity (UV and visible light)
for photocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction. Furthermore, during controlled HF etching of Ti3AlC2,

columns: TiO2 NPs were produced, thus, it can be activated by the light irradiations, producing electrons (and holes. The photogenerated electrons from CB of TiO2 (-0.52 eV) would be transferred towards)
rows: VB of g-C3N4, enabling their efficient separation. However, this mechanism would be limited
compared to g-C3N4 activation due to the presence of only small portion of TiO2 NPs over the
Ti3C2 surface.
According to thermodynamics, 8 electrons are required for CO2 reduction to CH4 compared to
only 2 electrons involvement for CO production. When UV-cut filters were employed, light
intensity was also reduced, whereas, only g-C3N4 was activated for the production of charge
carriers. In this case, lower number of electrons would be generated, resulting in production of CO
as the major product. Conversely, when visible light without UV-cut flirters was employed, light
intensity would be increased, whereas, it has potential to activate g-C3N4 and TiO2 NPs produced
over the Ti3C2 layers, resulting in more production of electrons. Due to proficient production of
charge carriers, CO2 was effectively converted to CO and CH4 with the involvement of 2 and 8
electrons, respectively. Besides, CO would also be converted to CH4 with the utilization of 6
electrons, resulting in more production of methane. Previously, MoS2 and Ti3C2 MXene as
cocatalyst for enhanced photoactivity of TiO2 for photocatalytic hydrogen production has been
reported [53]. Thus, a mixture of UV and visible light is more promising to maximize CO2

3.2.3 Effect of CO2/H2O feed ratios
The performance of g-C3N4/Bt/Ti3C2 composite catalyst was further investigated by varying
CO2/H2O feed ratio under the same operating conditions. It could be noted that CO2 was bubbled
through the water saturator and amount of water vapors carry by CO2 were dependent on the vapor
pressure of water. Using lower water temperature, CO2 would carry lower water vapors and higher
CO2/H2O feed ratio would be obtained. Conversely, using higher water temperature, more vapors
would be produced, thus CO2 carry more water vapors at high temperature and lower CO2/H2O
feed ratio is achieved. For getting different amounts of water vapors in a CO2 feed stream, the
water saturator temperature was varied from 15 to 45 oC under constant CO2 flow rate (20 mL min-
1) and catalyst loading (0.15 g). The performance analysis of g-C3N4/Bt/Ti3C2 was calculated based
on production of CO and CH4 under different irradiation times.

CO2/H2O feed ratios) have been demonstrated in Fig. 9. Production of CO in Fig. 9 (a) revels feed

During photocatalysis, uptake of CO2 and water should be attached to catalyst active sites for
proficient reduction and oxidation process. With feed temperature of 15oC, higher CO2/H2O feed
ratio in reactor system, resulting in more amount of CO2 attached to catalyst surface compared to
water. Under such conditions, majority of the active sites are occupied by the CO2 molecules,
whereas water molecules have to compete with CO2 for the adsorption. Thus, amount of water
attached to catalyst surface would not be enough to carry proficient oxidation process, resulting in
lower production of protons (H+) and more charge carrier recombination. However, when
temperature was increased to 45oC, lower CO2/H2O feed ratio was achieved. This shows, water
vapor rich CO2 feed mixture was passed through reactor to saturate the catalyst surface. Under
such condition, there would be more attachment of water molecules with catalyst active sites,
resulting in lower photo-activity. This was obviously, CO2 has to compete with water molecules
for its adsorption, and if lower amount of CO2 is attached with catalyst surface, reduction reaction
would be slowed down, resulting in lower efficiency. Highest amount of CO and CH4 were
produced at temperature 30 oC, probably both CO2 and H2O would be attached to catalyst surface,
resulting in proficient oxidation and reduction reaction with lower charge carrier recombination

CH4 was significantly enhanced under the same reaction conditions. The CH4 production over g-
C3N4/Bt/Ti3C2 composited was 4.15, 17.36 and 28.93 folds higher than using g-C3N4/Bt/Ti3C2, g-
C3N4/Ti3C2 and g-C3N4 samples, respectively. Similarly, a selectivity of 72.35 % was obtained
over g-C3N4/Bt/Ti3C2 for CH4 evolution, while it was 41.37, 14.95 and 30.28 % over g-
C3N4/Bt/Ti3C2, g-C3N4/Ti3C2 and g-C3N4, respectively, using CO2-water reaction system. This
selective photocatalytic CO2 conversion to CH4 suggests that g-C3N4/Bt/Ti3C2 is a promising
material and can be further explored in solar energy applications. The stability test revealed
continuous CO and CH4 evolution in cycles. The thermodynamics analysis elucidates, CO2 was
first converted to CO before the production of CH4 and water is oxidized to hydrogen under light
irradiation. These encourages results and new findings would be useful for further investigation in
this field for wastewater and solar energy applications.

Abstract: The selectivity of photocatalytic CO2 reduction to CH4 can be enhanced over Pt-
C A
decorated semiconductors, which is commonly attributed to the fact that a Schottky junction
is formed,
thus enhancing photoinduced electron
lifetime. However,
it
is difficult
to
understand why the yield of CO-the other product of photocatalytic CO2 reduction-is
decreased only in terms of photoinduced electron lifetime. In this work, the mechanism of
Pt-promoted CH4 formation was probed again in a gas-solid system of photocatalytic CO2

columns: reduction over highly-dispersed-Pt decorated In2O3 nanorods (Pt/In2O3). It was found that the
rows: presence of Pt modulates the surface property of In2O3 due to electronic and steric effect,
resulting in a loss of HCO3 -, b-CO3 2- and m-CO3 2- species for the coadsorption of CO2 with
H2O. However, this is not directly related with the high CH4 selectivity and low CO yield on
the Pt/In2O3 photocatalysts. Photocatalytic reductions of CO, HCOOH, CH2O, and CH3OH
as well as photocatalytic CO2 reduction over photocatalysts with different H2 uptakes confirm
that H adatoms derived from H2 or H2O dissociation on Pt play a key role in the formation of T
CH4. Low H2 dissociation barrier on Pt and weak H-Pt bond facilitate the bonding of C in P
CO2 with H, thus restraining CO production. In other words, the metallic Pt acts as atomic I R
hydrogen reservoir that supplies sufficient and readily available protons for CH4 formation
over Pt-decorated semiconductors. The present work offers a new window to explore non- C
noble metals or their alloys with stability in air and high dissociation ability to H2 or H2O as S U
a replacement of Pt for CO2 photoreduction to CH4.
Keywords: Photocatalytic CO2 reduction; metallic Pt; the selectivity to CH4 production; N
atomic hydrogen reservoir. A

rows: selectivity to CH4 production is hardly achieved over most photocatalysts.[10]
Several strategies have been proposed to enhance CH4 production selectivity, such as
surface modifications, ion dopings, developing new type catalysts and metal cocatalysts. For
example, hydrophobic modification of TiO2-SiO2 surface was used to enhance CO2
adsorption, thus facilitating the selective generation of CH4 from CO2;[4] Tahir and coworkers T P
demonstrated that doping In(III) in TiO2 remarkably increased the yield of CH4, which was ascribed to effective charge separation and inhibited recombination of photogenerated I R
electron-hole pairs.[11] Some unconventional photocatalysts, such as LaPO4 nanorods,3
Zn2GeO4 Nanoribbons,[12] SAPO-5 nanosheets,[13] β-SiC,[14] and so on,[15,16] were explored C
and exhibited a relatively high CH4 production selectivity. Among the above stated strategies, S U
metal cocatalyst has been a popular technique since Kraeutler and Bard first introduced Pt
onto TiO2 for photocatalytic CO2 reduction in 1978.[17,18] Up to now, it was also found that N
the enhanced CH4 production selectivity was obtained using other noble metals (such as Pd, A
Ru, Rh, Ag and Ir) as cocatalysts with a common character of high chemical stability in air.[5,19] For Pt-semconductor photocatalysts, the enhanced CH4 production selectivity is M
usually attributed to an increase in photoinduced electron lifetime, owning to the formation D E
of Schottky junctions at the Pt-semconductor interface.[20-24] Note the fact that the CO yield
is decreased accompanying the increase in CH4 production selectivity. In principle, CO yield T
should be also increased when the number of photoinduced electrons was increased on the P E
surface of Pt-semconductor photocatalysts, since the generation of CO is dynamically more
favorable. Moreover, there is no evidence indicating that the decreased CO yield was C
attributed to the fast transformation of CO to CH4.[24] In other words, the experimental C A
observations of the high selectivity to CH4 production and low CO yield can not be fully explained in terms of the photoinduced electron lifetime at Pt-semconductor interfaces.
In the present work, highly-dispersed-Pt decorated In2O3 nanorods with a conduction-
band bottom potential energy of - 0.62 eV vs. NHE were prepared using a wet chemical

columns: method in conjunction with photodeposition, where an acid and alkali neutralization reaction
rows: of In(OH)3 with H2PtCl6 was involved to enhance Pt dispersion. The mechanism of Pt-
promoted CH4 formation were explored again in a gas-solid system of photocatalytic CO2
reduction. The addition of Pt leads to a loss of bicarbonates, bidentated carbonate and
monodentated carbonate species for the coadsorption of CO2 with H2O on the surface of
In2O3. However, this is not related with the high CH4 selectivity and reduced CO yield over
Pt/In2O3. The photocatalytic reductions of the intermediate products of CO2 reduction such T
as CO, HCOOH, CH2O, and CH3OH as well as photocatalytic CO2 reduction over P
photocatalysts with different H2 uptakes confirm that H adatoms derived from dissociation I
adsorption of H2 or H2O reactant on metallic Pt play a key role in CH4 formation, which, plus R C
the prolonged photoinduced electron lifetime, would well explain the experimental S
observations of the enhanced selectivity to CH4 and low CO yield over Pt/In2O3.

2.2 Photocatalyst characterization
The chemical compositions of the prepared photocatalysts were analyzed by an ARL-
9800 X-ray fluorescence spectrometer (XRF). The surface area and pore size were
determined using an Autosorb-IQ-MP autosorption analyzer (Quantachrome), carried out at
77.3 K using N2 as an adsorbate. The samples were degassed at 473 K for 2 h before T
P
measurements. Pore size distribution curves were derived from the branch of adsorption I
isotherms. X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the samples were collected under ambient R
atmosphere by a Bruker D8 powder diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation (λ =1.5408 A) C
generated at 40 kV and 30 mA. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) characterization S U
was performed on a JEOL-JEM 2100 electron microscope. N
UV-vis diffuse reflectance spectra (DRS) over a range of 200-800 nm were recorded on
a UV-vis spectrophotometer (ShimadzuSolidSpec-3700DUV) with an integration sphere A
diffuse reflectance attachment. The energy band gaps of the as-prepared samples were calculated using (αhν)n = κ(hν-Eg), where α is the absorption coefficient, κ is the parameter M
related to the effective masses associated with the valence and conduction bands, n is 1/2 for D
the indirect transition, hν is the absorption energy, and Eg is the band gap energy. Plotting E
(αhν)1/2 versus hν based on the spectral response gives the extrapolated intercept T
corresponding to the Eg value. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) study was performed P
using a VG Microtech MT500 with an Mg-KX-ray source. All binding energies were E
referenced to carbon (1s) at 285.6 eV. Time resolved luminescence intensity decays at 395 nm were recorded on a HORIBA Fluorolog-3 molecule fluorometer (France). Those samples C C
were excited by a 300 nm laser light. A IR spectra for the coadsorption of CO2 and H2O were recorded with a Nicolet (IS50)
spectrophotometer (MCT detector) in the range 4000-1000 cm-1 with a resolution of 4 cm-1.
The self-supporting wafers (15-20 mg) were annealed in an IR cell at 473 K in Ar for 2 h

columns: and evacuated at the same temperature for 1 h. After the IR cell was cooled, CO2 and H2O
rows: vapor were introduced into the cell.
Adsorptions of H2 were carried out in a home-made volumetric adsorption system at
room temperature. The catalysts were evacuated at 473 K for 2 h before the measurements.
After cooling the catalysts to room temperature, doses of H2 were admitted sequentially and
the coverage of H2 was measured until the equilibrium pressure reached at about 14 kPa. The
uptake of H2 for the saturation coverage on a photo-catalyst surface was determined by T P
extrapolating the coverage of isotherm to P(H2)= 0. I
2.3 Photoactivity tests R C
Photocatalytic reductions were carried out in a reactor system connected to a vacuum
pump, and a 500 W Hg lamp was used as the light source with a light intensity of 0.120 W S
cm-2. For each test, 20 mg of a sample catalyst powder was evenly deposited on a circular U N
